idiom_name: class template parameterized by a LOCK policy type, with lock_guard/scoped_lock as the guard
implementation_notes: The pattern's original C++ form: give the component a LOCK template parameter and hold an instance of it as a private member, so the concurrency configuration is a compile-time typedef - FileCache<NullMutex>, FileCache<std::mutex>, FileCache<std::shared_mutex>. std::mutex, std::recursive_mutex and std::shared_mutex supply the policy family while std::lock_guard and std::scoped_lock (C++17) supply Scoped Locking, so only the parameterization is written by hand. The template form is still justified where the policy must be zero-overhead (an inlined no-op disappears entirely) or is fixed at build time; when the policy has to be chosen at run time, use the polymorphic variant instead.
pitfalls: The LOCK parameter is obtrusive: it appears in the component's type and therefore in every caller's signature; hide it behind an alias so applications never name the policy.

A non-recursive policy plus intra-component calls self-deadlocks while a recursive one silently doubles lock overhead - keep the Thread-Safe Interface split (public methods lock, _i methods assume held).
std::lock_guard cannot be moved and has no try-lock or timed lock; use std::unique_lock or std::scoped_lock when the policy needs those capabilities.

variants.name: Runtime lock policy through a Bridge handle
variants.idiom_name: abstract Lockable (acquire/release) plus a non-polymorphic Lock handle holding a Lockable&
variants.implementation_notes: The second form documented for the pattern, used when the policy is not known until run time: an abstract Lockable declares acquire/release, concrete strategies implement them, and a small non-polymorphic Lock class stores a Lockable reference so that the scoped guard can keep taking the lock by reference - the Bridge construction Schmidt describes for the pattern's polymorphic variant. Choose it when configuration or a plugin decides the policy; accept one indirect call per critical section, and make the strategy object outlive every component and guard that references it.
pitfalls: The handle stores a reference, so the concrete Lockable must outlive every component and guard that uses it - a strategy rebuilt per request is a dangling reference waiting to happen.
Every critical section pays an indirect acquire and release and the policy is invisible at the call site; when that buys nothing, prefer the compile-time template variant.
The effective policy becomes a runtime property, so a component constructed with the wrong strategy object cannot be detected by the type system.
